routes.description: Establish that human sin violates God's holy law and that reconciliation coherently requires the gracious, substitutionary work of Christ rather than human moral accounting.
routes.successCriteria: The route is completed by grounding humanity's need in sin, connecting forgiveness to divine holiness and justice, and locating effective reconciliation in Christ's scripturally attested sacrifice.

motionBridge.description: Show that Christ's atonement is the coherent and scripturally grounded means by which God forgives while maintaining holiness and justice.

centralBridges.description: Establish that fallen humanity is unable to secure reconciliation through its own deeds or repentance.
Explain how substitution joins divine mercy to the vindication of God's law rather than suspending justice.
Connect Christ's priesthood and sacrifice to the Old Testament system and the wider biblical account.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish Spirit-produced obedience after salvation from deeds offered as its basis.
Account for the authority and coherence of the scriptural sources used to establish atonement.

routes.description: Establish that God coherently forgives sincere repentants directly and judges accountable deeds, while disputing the scriptural necessity and historical grounding of substitutionary atonement.
routes.successCriteria: The route is completed by grounding direct forgiveness and moral accounting in the Qur'an and biblical texts, while showing that inherited guilt and substitution are unnecessary or later doctrinal developments.

motionBridge.description: Show that repentance, divine mercy, and accountable deeds provide a coherent and scripturally grounded account of sin and salvation without substitution.

centralBridges.description: Explain why principled direct forgiveness can remain consistent with divine holiness and justice.
Ground judgment in personal conduct rather than inherited guilt or an inability requiring substitution.
Show that biblical support for substitution reflects Pauline or later development rather than the original teaching of Jesus and earlier scripture.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve a material role for enabled human obedience and repentance in the account of salvation.
Explain the textual and transmission distinctions involved in appeals to the Qur'an and Bible.

sectionSelections.title: Direct forgiveness, holiness, and justice
sectionSelections.rationale: The motion centrally turns on whether forgiveness requires an objective satisfaction of divine law or can be granted directly through principled mercy.

proSelections.proposition: Because God's law reflects his holy nature, forgiveness must have a ground that preserves the connection between divine holiness and the law violated by sin.
Christ's substitutionary atonement permits God to extend mercy and grace without undoing justice or disregarding divine law.

conSelections.proposition: The Qur'an teaches that sincere repentance brings God's direct forgiveness and that final judgment accounts for human deeds.
God can forgive repentant sinners directly without violating holiness or justice when divine mercy is exercised on a principled rather than arbitrary basis.

sectionSelections.title: Human fallenness and personal responsibility
sectionSelections.rationale: Each route requires an account of the sinner's condition that determines whether accountable repentance is sufficient or supernatural liberation and representation are necessary.

proSelections.proposition: Adam's representative rebellion brought spiritual death, leaving fallen people unable to do good or come to Christ apart from supernatural grace.
Human enslavement to sin prevents people from coming to Christ without God's gracious drawing and liberating action.

conSelections.proposition: Genesis and the poetic language of the Psalms do not establish inherited original sin, while the Old Testament assigns people responsibility for their own conduct.
People need not be morally perfect to be judged righteous because, under God's merciful accounting, their good can outweigh their faults.

sectionSelections.title: The place of deeds in salvation
sectionSelections.rationale: The competing routes must explain scriptural commands and judgments concerning deeds while identifying whether obedience is a basis, condition, or result of salvation.

proSelections.proposition: Good deeds are produced by the Spirit as the result of complete redemption in Christ rather than contributions that earn or complete salvation.
Believers work out a salvation they already possess while God transforms them into people devoted to good deeds.

conSelections.proposition: Paul's references to judgment by deeds and James's treatment of faith and works preserve moral accounting that conflicts with justification through Christ's death.
Divine enablement does not remove a person's obligation to work out salvation and therefore does not make human action dispensable.

sectionSelections.title: The coherence and operation of atonement
sectionSelections.rationale: The atonement route must specify how Christ's role makes forgiveness coherent, while the direct-forgiveness route disputes whether punishment or payment through an innocent substitute is intelligible.

proSelections.proposition: Hebrews presents Jesus as both the Melchizedekian high priest and the offered sacrifice whose resurrection gives his single offering permanent efficacy.
Jesus's identity as the sinless God-man enables his sacrifice for sin, and salvation transforms believers' hearts so that obedience follows.

conSelections.proposition: Substitutionary and victory accounts are incoherent when they portray God as punishing his innocent son, receiving payment from him, or offering him as bait for Satan.
People begin in a naturally saved disposition and, after deliberate rejection, can return through sincere repentance, restitution, and God's direct forgiveness without another person paying for sin.

sectionSelections.title: Scriptural continuity and doctrinal development
sectionSelections.rationale: Because the motion asks which account is scripturally grounded, each route must connect its salvation model to earlier scripture and explain the provenance of later atonement claims.

proSelections.proposition: The repeated Day of Atonement sacrifices prefigure Christ's unique effective sacrifice, which obtains eternal redemption and fulfills the Old Testament system.
The Bible consistently teaches that the holy and just God provides the sole means of reconciliation through Christ's accepted sacrifice and resurrection.

conSelections.proposition: The Old Testament supports obedience, repentance, and divine forgiveness without making blood payment or Christ's substitutionary death necessary.
Substitutionary justification is chiefly Pauline and gains support in later Gospels, making its attribution to Jesus historically questionable.
